Family Research Council 
801 G Street NW, Washington, D.C. 20001 | frc.org | (202) 393-2100 
 
September 3, 2025 
 
Submitted electronically 
The Honorable Douglas A. Collins  
Secretary 
U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs  
810 Vermont Avenue, NW 
Washington, DC 20420 
 
Re:  
Public comment regarding the proposal to “reinstate the full exclusion on abortions 
and abortion counseling from the medical benefits package” and “the exclusions on 
abortion and abortion counseling for Civilian Health and Medical Program of the 
Department of Veterans Affairs (CHAMPVA) that were removed in 2022.” 
RIN: 2900-AS31 
 
Dear Secretary Collins: 
 
Family Research Council (FRC) is a nonprofit research and educational organization dedicated to 
articulating and advancing a family-centered philosophy of public life. Our vision is a prevailing 
culture in which all human life is valued, families flourish, and religious liberty thrives. We 
respectfully submit the following comment in support of the proposed rule that would restore the U.S. 
Department of Veterans Affairs’ (VA) medical benefits package and CHAMPVA benefits to what they 
were before long-standing protections from abortion were removed in 2022. 
 
The proposed rule correctly recognizes that it is never medically necessary to intentionally kill an 
unborn child to save a mother’s life. Physicians are never required to compromise their commitment to 
one of their patients (the unborn child) for the sake of the other (the mother) and vice versa.1 
 
The misconception that abortion is sometimes medically necessary to save the life of the mother stems 
from misinformation spread by the pro-abortion lobby with the intention of instilling fear in the general 
public. Prior to the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization 
(2022), it was widely accepted that miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy treatment, and early induction to 
save a mother’s life are all markedly different from the act of intentionally killing an unborn child. 
However, following the Dobbs decision, the pro-abortion lobby endeavored to make the public conflate 
them. 
 
The Problem: Confusing Definitions 
 
At the root of the issue is the definitional uncertainty of the word “abortion.” The medical community’s 
terminology complicates the matter. In medical terms, an abortion is the ending of an intrauterine 
pregnancy prior to 20 weeks, regardless of the cause. According to the American Academy of 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
2 
Professional Coders, there are nine common types of abortion: complete, elective, incomplete, induced, 
inevitable, missed, septic, spontaneous, and therapeutic.2  
 
Several of these medical terms (i.e., spontaneous, missed, inevitable, incomplete, and complete) are 
used to describe what is colloquially referred to as miscarriage. This has resulted in pro-abortionists 
arguing that abortion is a necessary component of women’s health care. They contend that if a 
miscarriage and the necessary procedures surrounding it that ensure all parts of the pregnancy have 
been removed from the mother are all part of an abortion, then an abortion is not always a choice, and 
it is a part of health care. 
 
However, this confusion surrounding the term “abortion” is manufactured. Both the medical 
community and the general public understand that medical terminology is not used when speaking 
colloquially about the intentional killing of an unborn child. The bi-annual study on “abortion” 
conducted by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) serves as evidence of this 
understanding. 
 
When conducting its “Abortion Surveillance,” the CDC uses the definition of “induced abortion” to 
describe an abortion: 
 
[A]n intervention performed within the limits of state and jurisdiction law by a licensed 
clinician (e.g., a physician, nurse-midwife, nurse practitioner, or physician assistant) intended to 
terminate a suspected or known intrauterine pregnancy and that does not result in a live birth. 
This definition excludes management of intrauterine fetal death, early pregnancy failure or loss, 
ectopic pregnancy, or retained products of conception. All abortions in this report are 
considered to be legally induced unless stated otherwise.3 
 
The pro-abortion American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) defines abortion as 
“An intervention to end a pregnancy so that it does not result in a live birth.”4  
 
Both the CDC and ACOG definitions acknowledge that the purpose of an induced abortion is to 
produce a dead child. Typically, when people talk about “abortion” or “the right to an abortion,” they 
are referring to induced abortion.  
 
A Solution: Better Definitions 
 
The American Association of Pro-Life Obstetricians and Gynecologists (AAPLOG) defines induced 
abortion as:  
 
• The use of any drug, device, surgery, or any procedure or intervention with the purpose of 
ensuring the death of the living human being in utero before, during, or in the process of 
separating the mother and her embryo or fetus. 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
3 
• Any pre-viable separation of the mother and the living embryo or fetus in utero without 
proportional danger of maternal death or permanent irreversible damage to one or more of her 
major body systems.5  
 
Categorizing induced abortion in this way clarifies what induced abortion is not: 
 
• The removal of an embryo or fetus who has died of natural causes and/or the removal of 
placental tissue or remaining parts of the embryo or fetus after an incomplete induced abortion 
is not an induced abortion. 
• The separation of a mother and embryo or viable or pre-viable fetus in cases of threat to the life 
of the mother, such as ectopic pregnancy, sepsis, and other critical maternal illness prior to 
viability, which cannot be managed in any other way, is not an induced abortion, since the 
intent of the separation is not the death of the embryo or fetus. This is consistent with the 
CDC’s definition of induced abortion.6 
 
Since the above circumstances are not abortion, abortion is never medically necessary to save the life 
of the mother. 
 
Real Health Care Strives to Help Both Mother and Baby 
 
A mother’s life and physical well-being are of utmost importance and should be the primary focus of 
physicians when addressing medical complications during pregnancy. As the proposed rule recognizes, 
prioritizing a mother’s life and well-being and treating the unborn child that she is carrying with equal 
dignity and respect are not mutually exclusive.  
 
Unfortunately, there are tragic circumstances in which women cannot continue their pregnancies due to 
medical complications. These complications may include ectopic pregnancy,7 cancer, infection, heart 
problems, placental abruption, or severe preeclampsia. In such cases, as AAPLOG notes, treating the 
mother for the condition does not constitute an abortion.  
 
Thanks to advances in medicine, it may be possible to save an unborn child’s life even when mother 
and baby are in distress. In the 1970s, the age of viability was around 28 weeks.8 Today, due to 
advancements in fetal medicine, the youngest recorded survivor was born at just 21 weeks.9 This 
means that when a physician needs to induce labor to treat a mother’s condition, the baby has a chance 
of surviving seven weeks earlier than was possible in the 1970s. Additionally, improvements in 
technology have allowed physicians to monitor a mother’s condition more closely and recognize when 
life-saving action must be taken. 
 
Still, there may be situations in which preterm induction or early delivery is necessary to save the 
mother’s life. Tragically, if the delivery takes place prior to 21 weeks, the baby is unlikely to survive. 
But, again, as AAPLOG notes, these are not abortions. An induced abortion intentionally and directly 
ends a child’s life, while a preterm induction is not intended to end the child’s life. In the case of a 
preterm induction, a child’s death is seen as a tragic loss rather than an intended outcome. 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
4 
Some have voiced concerns that in jurisdictions where laws protect unborn children from abortion, 
doctors might hesitate to provide care that could result in the death of the unborn child, fearing legal 
repercussions. But such fears are born out of confusion cultivated by the pro-abortion lobby. All 
existing pro-life protections in the United States explicitly state that they do not prevent medical 
procedures necessary to save a mother’s life. Any doctor—military or civilian—who refuses to provide 
care to a mother is offering substandard, unacceptable health care.10 
 
Conclusion 
 
The VA’s proposed rule to reinstate full protections from abortion is a welcome change that aligns with 
providing top-quality medical care for those who have served or are serving our country. FRC is 
grateful to the Trump administration for taking this important step toward ensuring our military 
protects and defends the innocent and vulnerable, including those in the womb.  
 
Respectfully submitted, 
 
/s/ Mary Szoch, M.Ed. 
Director of the Center for Human Dignity 
 
/s/ Chris Gacek, Ph.D., J.D. 
Senior Fellow for Regulatory Affairs 
 
Family Research Council 
801 G Street, NW 
Washington, DC 20001
